Jābāli Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a short, minor, Upaniṣad belonging to the Sāmaveda and is classed among the Śaiva उपनिषद्स्.
It is in the form of a dialogue between the sages Paippalādi and जाबालि. It contains 23 mantras, all in prose.
The questions asked concern four topics: जीव, पशु, Īśa and the means of मोक्ष.
Jābāli, the teacher got the knowledge about them from षडानन (the six faced सुब्रह्मण्य) who in turn, got it from his ड़थेर् ईशान (Īśvara or शिव) by worshipping him.
Īśvara is पशुपति (literally, ‘the lord of animals or living beings’). Somehow, due to the association with अहङ्कार or egoism, he himself becomes the paśus (the animals or the bound souls).
The jīvas or the individual souls—like animals—lack discrimination and are driven to do things by others. Hence they are called paśus. Being the lord of these jīvas and all-knowing, ईश्वर has been called ‘Paśupati’.
How does one get the knowledge of that Īśa? By wearing the भस्म or holy ash at the appropriate places like the head, the forehead, chest and so on, using the pañca-brahma-mantras (mantras containing the names of the five aspects of शिव or ईश्वर, viz., सद्योजात, वामदेव, अघोर, Tatpuruṣa, and ईशान). Drawing the three lines (tripuṇḍra) is called ‘śāmbhavavrata’.
This is then followed by what these three lines represent. They stand for: the three Vedic fires, the three worlds, the three extractions of the सोम juice and the three syllables of ओङ्कार (a, u, and m).
The Upaniṣad concludes with the eulogy that one who wears the three lines of विभूति or भस्म will be liberated from all sins. He is as good as having studied the वेदस्, as good as having perfect meditation, as good as having bathed in all the sacred rivers and as good as having repeated all the mantras of God रुद्र.
And, he will not return to mundane existence again.
See also UPANIṢADS.

Jābāli
------------------------------------------
According to the Mahābhārata he was one of the sons of the sage विश्वामित्र but was more closely associated with the sage वसिष्ठ.
In the Rāmāyaṇa (Ayodhyākāṇḍa 106) जाबालि has been described as one of the eight priests of the king दशरथ. When राम went to the forest, he accompanied भरत, along with वसिष्ठ, to try to bring him back. As भरत’s entreaties to राम fell on deaf ears, जाबालि intervened. He tried to advise राम taking an extremely materialistic view. Since दशरथ was an old man lustful by nature, and since he was dead now, there was no need to take his words (or command) seriously! One need not bother much about the next world but enjoy the good things of life here and now, and so on!
Of course, he was interested in somehow bringing back राम to अयोध्या and was not really an atheist or agnostic.

Jābāla Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
One of the well-known minor उपनिषद्स् assigned to the Atharvaveda (or the Śukla Yajurveda according to some), the Jābāla Upaniṣad is in prose and deals mainly with the subject of renunciation and मोनस्तिचिस्म्. It is, practically, the only Upaniṣad that allows a person to take to the life of सṁन्यास even from the first or the second stage of life (i.e., from the ब्रह्मचर्य आश्रम or the गृहस्थ आश्रम), the sole criterion being intense renunciation.
There are six khaṇḍas or sections, each containing one long passage in prose. Some versions divide these passages into smaller units, the total number being twelve.
The Upaniṣad starts with a short dialogue between बृहस्पति and Yājña-valkya. बृहस्पति extols the greatness of Avimuktakṣetra (i.e., काशी or वाराणसी, the modern Banaras in Uttar Pradesh) calling it as कुरुक्षेत्र also. Its greatness is mainly due to the fact that रुद्र (Śiva) teaches the ‘tārakamantra’ (Rāmanāma) to all the jīvas who give up their bodies there.
In the next section, in reply to the question raised by the sage अत्रि, Yājña-valkya teaches the method of upāsanā or meditation on the avimukta (the Self) established between varaṇā and nāśī (i.e., in between the eyebrows and above the nose). This point is the meeting place of the world of gods and the world beyond.
Then, while answering the questions raised by some brahmacārins or Vedic students, याज्ञवल्क्य eulogises the Śatarudriya—same as the Rudrādhyāya of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda—and advises them to meditate on it, as also the names and the forms of रुद्र described by it.
Janaka, the king of Videha, approaches याज्ञवल्क्य and requests him to teach about सṁन्यास or the life of renunciation. After first describing how a person has to take to the next आश्रम or stage of life, completing the previous one, याज्ञवल्क्य declares that one can take to the life of सṁन्यास directly even from the earlier stages like ब्रह्मचर्य or गार्हस्थ्य, provided there is intense वैराग्य or spirit of renunciation.
This is followed by some details of the process of taking सṁन्यास which include the ceremonial abandonment of the Vedic fire and repetition of the प्रणव or Om.
In the next section, in reply to a question by the sage अत्रि, याज्ञवल्क्य replies that a saṁnyāsin need not wear the यज्ञोपवीत (the sacred thread) since he purifies himself by आचमन (ceremonial sipping of water with appropriate mantras) which is a part of the procedure for taking सṁन्यास.
It is interesting to note that the Upaniṣad permits religious सुइचिदे for one who is disgusted with worldly life, but is unfit or unable to take सṁन्यास. This can take the form of drowning in water or entering into a blazing fire or even dying on the battle field.
Taking सṁन्यास mentally has also been permitted for those who are physically unfit for formal सṁन्यास.
The last section describes the life-pattern of paramahaṁsas, the paragons of the monastic ideal, like Saṁvartaka, आरुणि, श्वेतकेतु, Durvāsa, Ṛbhu, दत्तात्रेय, जडभरत and others.
Since they are paramahaṁsas (monks of the highest order), they do not carry any external insignia of सṁन्यास with them. They move about freely, begging for alms when hungry and live in deserted places like empty and forsaken houses, river-banks, hills, caves and so on. They are ever devoted to the आत्मन् inside and give up their bodies without the least attachment to them.
See also UPANIṢADS.
